nearly.text: Long before she led the city orchestra, Elena Ruiz [[conducted]] a study of how the shape of a concert hall affects the sound of a violin.
nearly.clue: a study of how the shape of a concert hall affects

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The census of 1790 was [[conducted]] by federal marshals and their assistants, who traveled on horseback to count every household.
nearly.clue: who traveled on horseback to count every household

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: The bandmaster's widow [[conducted]] the inquiry into the missing silver herself, questioning each servant in turn.
nearly.clue: questioning each servant in turn

partners: conduct a study / a survey / an interview

lookalikes.tell: Conduct means carry out; a conduit is a channel through which something flows.

meaning: Unfriendly or lacking enthusiasm, as in “a cool reception.”
examples: The proposal received a [[cool]] response from the council, and it was quietly dropped.
Her tone was polite but [[cool]], and he knew he had offended her.

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: The new dress was in the latest style, but Lady Ann's [[cool]] glance at it told her niece that she disapproved.
nearly.clue: told her niece that she disapproved

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: Europe's rulers gave the young republic's envoy a [[cool]] reception; none would meet with him, and most would not answer his letters.
nearly.clue: none would meet with him

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The physicist's colleagues were [[cool]] toward her new theory at first, and none agreed to test it until she had published two more papers.
nearly.clue: none agreed to test it

lookalikes.tell: Cool means unfriendly or unenthusiastic; coy means pretending to be shy.

meaning: Extremely important, because much depends on it.
examples: The next forty-eight hours will be [[critical]] for the patient.
Bees play a [[critical]] role in pollinating many crops.

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Some reviewers of the report were harsh, but all agreed on one point: wetlands are [[critical]] to the survival of migrating birds, which rely on them for food and rest.
nearly.clue: which rely on them for food and rest

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: Control of the river was [[critical]] to both armies, since whoever held it could move supplies and troops at will.
nearly.clue: since whoever held it could move supplies and troops at will

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Though Aunt Jane found fault with everything else, she admitted that the letter had come at a [[critical]] moment: one more day and the house would have been sold.
nearly.clue: one more day and the house would have been sold

lookalikes.tell: Critical here means crucial; a critique is a detailed evaluation of a work.

meaning: Shy and tending to avoid attention or company.
everyday: stopping work at the end of a career
examples: A [[retiring]] man, the inventor rarely gave interviews.
Despite her fame, the poet remained [[retiring]], seldom leaving her house.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: Although he was only thirty and far from the end of his career, the [[retiring]] clerk avoided every public meeting and left the speeches to others.
nearly.clue: avoided every public meeting

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The chemist was so [[retiring]] that she let a colleague present their joint discovery, and for years few people knew her part in it.
nearly.clue: let a colleague present their joint discovery

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Everyone expected old Mr. Todd to give a grand speech on his last day at the bank, but, [[retiring]] as ever, he slipped out early without saying goodbye.
nearly.clue: he slipped out early without saying goodbye

lookalikes.tell: Retiring means shy; tiring means exhausting.

meaning: A person's or a group's status or reputation in the eyes of others.
examples: The scandal damaged the senator's [[standing]] with voters.
The discovery raised the young scientist's [[standing]] among her colleagues.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The general was the last officer still on his feet at the end of the battle, and his [[standing]] with the troops rose so high that they later urged him to run for president.
nearly.clue: rose so high that they later urged him to run for president

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Publishing in the journal did much for the young lab's [[standing]]: within a year, it was receiving invitations to speak at major conferences.
nearly.clue: it was receiving invitations to speak at major conferences

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Mrs. Frost had stood at the church door every Sunday for thirty years, and her [[standing]] in the village was such that no family dared hold a wedding without inviting her.
nearly.clue: no family dared hold a wedding without inviting her

partners: standing in the community / with voters / in good standing

lookalikes.tell: Standing is status or reputation; a stance is a position on an issue.

meaning: To take something for one's own use, often without permission; also, to set money aside for a particular purpose.
examples: The settlers [[appropriated]] land that had long been used by the region's first peoples.
Congress [[appropriated]] funds for the new dam.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The new government [[appropriated]] the church's lands and sold them to pay its war debts.
nearly.clue: and sold them to pay its war debts

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Modernist poets freely [[appropriated]] lines from older writers, weaving borrowed phrases into their own verse.
nearly.clue: weaving borrowed phrases into their own verse

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Cuckoos [[appropriate]] the nests of other species, laying their eggs there and leaving the owners to raise the chicks.
nearly.clue: laying their eggs there and leaving the owners to raise the chicks

lookalikes.tell: Appropriate means take for one's own use; apportion means divide and share out.

meaning: Stated clearly and directly rather than suggested; also, specific, as in “for the express purpose.”
examples: The will stated her [[express]] wish that the house become a library.
The land was sold for the [[express]] purpose of building a school.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The railroad was built at great speed, but the charter's [[express]] terms forbade the company to run trains on Sundays.
nearly.clue: terms forbade the company to run trains on Sundays

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Against her father's [[express]] command, Clara took the fast mail coach to the city alone.
nearly.clue: command

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The drug was approved only for the [[express]] purpose of treating adults; its use in children had never been studied.
nearly.clue: its use in children had never been studied

lookalikes.tell: Express means clearly stated; expressive means full of feeling.

meaning: Completely obvious; clear to anyone who looks.
everyday: a legal right to an invention
examples: The claim was a [[patent]] falsehood, easily disproved by the records.
Her discomfort was [[patent]] to everyone at the table.

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The inventor's application was rejected for a [[patent]] reason: a nearly identical machine had been on sale for a decade.
nearly.clue: a nearly identical machine had been on sale for a decade

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The treaty's unfairness was [[patent]]: one side gave up half its territory and received nothing in return.
nearly.clue: one side gave up half its territory and received nothing in return

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: His boredom at the recital was [[patent]]; he yawned openly and checked his watch every few minutes.
nearly.clue: he yawned openly and checked his watch every few minutes

lookalikes.tell: Patent means obvious; potent means powerful.

meaning: To grow larger, stronger or more intense; the opposite of “wane.”
examples: The moon [[waxes]] for about two weeks before it is full.
His enthusiasm for the project [[waxed]] as the first results came in.

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The beekeeper, who collected wax from her hives each fall, noticed that the colony's strength [[waxed]] and waned with the supply of clover.
nearly.clue: and waned with the supply of clover

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The empire's power [[waxed]] for two centuries before it began its long decline.
nearly.clue: before it began its long decline

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: As the evening wore on and the candles burned down, the old captain's stories [[waxed]] ever more daring, until no one at the table believed a word.
nearly.clue: ever more daring

lookalikes.tell: Wax means grow; waive means give up a right.

meaning: To praise someone or something publicly and enthusiastically; often used as “hailed as.”
everyday: call out to, as to stop a taxi
examples: Critics [[hailed]] the novel as the finest of the decade.
The treaty was [[hailed]] as a turning point in relations between the two nations.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: When the battered ship sailed back into the harbor, crowds lined the docks to [[hail]] its crew as heroes of the voyage.
nearly.clue: as heroes of the voyage

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Doctors [[hailed]] the vaccine as a triumph, since it cut cases of the disease by ninety percent in its first year.
nearly.clue: as a triumph

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: The villagers, who had once mocked the young poet, now [[hailed]] her as their greatest daughter.
nearly.clue: who had once mocked the young poet

lookalikes.tell: Hail means praise publicly; hale means healthy and strong.

meaning: Offering or containing less than usual; meager, as in “lean years” or “a lean budget.”
examples: The farm barely survived the [[lean]] years of the drought.
The company kept a [[lean]] staff of only twelve people.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: During the [[lean]] winters of the 1780s, families in the valley survived on turnips and the little grain they had stored.
nearly.clue: survived on turnips and the little grain they had stored

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: In [[lean]] years, when acorns are scarce, the squirrels bury fewer nuts and raise fewer young.
nearly.clue: when acorns are scarce

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Resting his elbows on the fence, the old farmer described the [[lean]] seasons of his boyhood, when there was rarely meat on the table.
nearly.clue: when there was rarely meat on the table

partners: lean years / a lean budget / lean times

lookalikes.tell: Lean means meager; a lien is a legal claim on property until a debt is paid.

meaning: A basis or reason for a belief or an action; often used in the plural, as in “grounds for concern.”
examples: The court found no [[grounds]] for the lawsuit.
Is there any [[ground]] for believing the rumor?

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Soil samples taken near the factory gave the town [[grounds]] for concern: they contained ten times the lead allowed by law.
nearly.clue: they contained ten times the lead allowed by law

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The farmers' petition argued that the tax had no legal [[ground]], since it had never been approved by the assembly.
nearly.clue: since it had never been approved by the assembly

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Mrs. Webb suspected the new maid of stealing, but she had no [[grounds]] for it beyond a missing spoon that later turned up in the garden.
nearly.clue: beyond a missing spoon that later turned up in the garden

partners: grounds for concern / on the grounds that

lookalikes.tell: Grounds are reasons for a belief; grounded means sensible and realistic, or kept from going out.

meaning: Easily shaped or changed; able to be molded, as clay or a young brain is.
examples: The brain remains [[plastic]] throughout life, forming new connections as we learn.
Wet clay is [[plastic]]; once fired, it becomes rigid.

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Children's brains are especially [[plastic]], which helps explain why children pick up new languages more easily than adults do.
nearly.clue: which helps explain why children pick up new languages more easily

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: In the sculptor's hands, even the stubborn river clay became [[plastic]], taking the shape of a face in minutes.
nearly.clue: taking the shape of a face in minutes

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: For a few years after the revolution, the nation's institutions were [[plastic]], and reformers could reshape courts and schools with a single law.
nearly.clue: reformers could reshape courts and schools with a single law

partners: the brain is plastic / a plastic material

lookalikes.tell: Plastic means easily shaped; plaster is a paste that hardens on walls.

meaning: To think, speak or write about something at length, often more than is helpful; used as “dwell on.”
examples: The biography [[dwells]] on the composer's childhood and passes quickly over his later years.
Try not to [[dwell]] on mistakes you cannot undo.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: Historians of the city once [[dwelt]] on its wealthy merchants; newer studies turn to the dockworkers and servants who made that wealth possible.
nearly.clue: newer studies turn to the dockworkers and servants

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: In her letters, Grandmother [[dwells]] at length on the house where she was born, describing each room as if she still lived in it.
nearly.clue: describing each room as if she still lived in it

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: The report [[dwells]] on the risks of the new pesticide but says almost nothing about its benefits.
nearly.clue: but says almost nothing about its benefits

partners: dwell on the past / a mistake / a detail

lookalikes.tell: Dwell on means linger on a subject; dwindle means shrink little by little.

meaning: Able to judge quality well and to notice fine differences, as in “a discriminating reader.”
examples: A [[discriminating]] collector, she bought only a few paintings, but each was a masterpiece.
The shop is aimed at [[discriminating]] buyers willing to pay for handmade work.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: Unlike the other patrons at court, who bought whatever was fashionable, the duchess was a [[discriminating]] buyer of art, rejecting nine paintings for every one she kept.
nearly.clue: rejecting nine paintings for every one she kept

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Honeybees are [[discriminating]] foragers: they can tell apart flowers whose nectar differs in sugar by only a few percent, and they favor the sweeter ones.
nearly.clue: they can tell apart flowers whose nectar differs in sugar by only a few percent

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: The editor had a [[discriminating]] ear; she could hear at once which line in a poem was false, and she cut it without mercy.
nearly.clue: she could hear at once which line in a poem was false

lookalikes.tell: Discriminating means able to judge quality; discriminatory means treating people unfairly.

meaning: Striking and eye-catching; so interesting or unusual that it holds attention.
examples: The cover shows an [[arresting]] image: a single red boot standing in the snow.
Her essay opens with an [[arresting]] claim that most readers will want to dispute.

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: The detective novel opens with an [[arresting]] scene: a woman walks into a police station carrying a birdcage and asks to confess.
nearly.clue: a woman walks into a police station carrying a birdcage

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Among the telescope's first pictures was an [[arresting]] view of two galaxies colliding, their spiral arms twisted into long glowing streams.
nearly.clue: their spiral arms twisted into long glowing streams

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The mural's most [[arresting]] figure, a sheriff holding a lantern, was painted larger than any other and placed at the very center.
nearly.clue: was painted larger than any other and placed at the very center

lookalikes.tell: Arresting means striking and eye-catching; alarming means frightening or worrying.

meaning: Speed and efficiency in getting something done; usually used as “with dispatch.”
examples: The clerk handled every request with [[dispatch]], and the line never grew long.
The repairs were finished with a [[dispatch]] that surprised the whole town.

nearly.subject: history
nearly.text: The general's riders carried his orders with such [[dispatch]] that his officers often received them before the enemy had moved.
nearly.clue: that his officers often received them before the enemy had moved

nearly.subject: science
nearly.text: Once the leak was found, the engineers acted with [[dispatch]], sealing the pipe within an hour.
nearly.clue: sealing the pipe within an hour

nearly.subject: literature
nearly.text: Mrs. Hale packed the trunks and posted the letters with her usual [[dispatch]], and the family was on the road by noon.
nearly.clue: and the family was on the road by noon

lookalikes.tell: Dispatch is speed with efficiency; haste is speed that is often careless.
